1. Title

Project Title: LOANIQ: Retail Loan Underwriting & Approval Prediction System using Machine Learning with MLOps Telemetry, Local Explainability, and Algorithmic Fairness Surveillance

Academic Course: Machine Learning Mini-Project (Semester-I, Academic Year 2026-27)

Domain: Financial Machine Learning (FinTech), Supervised Classification, Model Interpretability (XAI), and Responsible AI Governance

Target Architecture: Production-ready FastAPI REST service paired with a clean, unclustered retail lending dashboard engineered for non-technical loan underwriting officers.

2. Abstract

Retail loan underwriting in commercial banking is traditionally characterized by labor-intensive manual assessments, lengthy turnaround times (often spanning 3 to 5 business days), subjective evaluation inconsistencies, and high operational costs. While machine learning offers significant potential to automate credit screening, models deployed in isolation without continuous observability risk catastrophic performance degradation under macroeconomic shifts, opaque black-box decisions violating regulatory disclosure requirements, and unintentional demographic bias.

To resolve these critical industrial challenges, this project develops LOANIQ, an enterprise-grade automated loan underwriting and decision intelligence system. Built upon the canonical 614-applicant retail credit benchmark, LOANIQ establishes an end-to-end MLOps pipeline comprising automated data quality profiling, leak-free preprocessing with custom Interquartile Range (IQR) outlier capping, and domain-specific financial feature engineering (Debt-to-Income, Equated Monthly Installment ratios, and Household Disposable Income). A comprehensive benchmark evaluating 12 diverse algorithms across stratified 5-fold cross-validation identifies the XGBoost Classifier as the optimal champion model, achieving 86.18% Test Accuracy, a 0.9071 Test F1-Score, an ROC-AUC of 0.8359, and an outstanding 97.65% Recall on creditworthy applicants.

Beyond raw prediction, LOANIQ integrates TreeSHAP to provide real-time local attributions translated into plain-English reasons for non-technical bank officers, asynchronous SQLite event telemetry with sub-30ms response times (exceeding the 500ms industrial SLA by 95%), automated macroeconomic drift surveillance using Population Stability Index (PSI) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and an ethical AI audit via Fairlearn MetricFrame ensuring strict Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) compliance (under 2% demographic disparity). The system is deployed via a dual interface: a robust FastAPI REST backend and an intuitive, uncluttered web dashboard designed specifically for non-technical retail lending stakeholders.

3. Introduction

Credit provision represents the foundational revenue-generating activity for commercial and retail banks worldwide. The fundamental challenge of credit underwriting consists of accurately distinguishing creditworthy borrowers who will service their debt reliably from high-risk applicants likely to default on repayment schedules. Historically, credit evaluation has relied upon manual underwriter reviews, committee discussions, and rigid rule-based scorecards. In modern digital economies, this paradigm suffers from several critical bottlenecks:

  • Prolonged Turnaround Times: Manual application assessment introduces delays of several days, creating customer friction and loan abandonment.
  • Inconsistent Risk Boundaries: Human underwriters often exhibit subjective evaluation variances across branch locations and personal risk tolerances.
  • Inability to Model Non-Linear Interactions: Complex joint interactions between borrower income, collateral property liquidity, family dependency burden, and loan amortization terms cannot be modeled adequately by simple linear scorecards.
  • The Regulatory "Black-Box" Dilemma: Financial regulations such as the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) legally mandate that banks provide explicit, non-discriminatory adverse action notices whenever credit is denied. Black-box deep learning or uninterpretable models cannot be deployed without local explainability.

The LOANIQ project bridges the gap between theoretical machine learning research and enterprise banking implementation. By implementing a full lifecycle ML architecture—from raw ingestion to model explainability, live inference telemetry, drift surveillance, and fairness auditing—LOANIQ demonstrates how responsible AI can streamline retail credit origination safely, transparently, and equitably.

4. Problem Statement

Retail banking institutions face the dual imperative of accelerating loan origination velocity while minimizing Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). Specifically, the technical and business problem can be articulated as follows:

Mathematical Formulation:
Given an applicant feature vector x ∈ ℜd containing financial, geographical, and demographic attributes, learn a mapping function f: x → y ∈ {0, 1} estimating the probability P(y=1|x) ≥ τ, where y=1 denotes loan approval and y=0 denotes rejection, subject to:
1. Maximizing classification accuracy and F1-score on minority default cases.
2. Enforcing sub-500ms inference latency SLA.
3. Generating faithful, local feature importance vectors φi(x) for regulatory transparency.
4. Constraining demographic disparity across protected groups: |P(ŷ=1|A=0) - P(ŷ=1|A=1)| ≤ εparity.

The core computational and domain challenges addressed in this work include:

  1. Class Imbalance: In retail loan portfolios, approved loans outnumber rejected applications by approximately 2.2:1 (68.7% vs 31.3%), requiring stratified evaluation to avoid majority-class bias.
  2. Severe Missingness & Skew: Critical fields such as Credit History (8.14% missing) and Self-Employment status contain missing entries, while Applicant Income spans from $150 to $81,000, creating heavy right-skew that distorts gradient-based optimization.
  3. Silent Data Drift: Economic shocks alter interest rates, borrower debt burdens, and income stabilities, causing unmonitored models to experience catastrophic degradation in real-world deployment.
  4. Proxy Discrimination: Even when protected attributes like gender or marital status are omitted from training inputs, correlated proxy features can reintroduce demographic bias, necessitating formal Fairlearn auditing.

5. Objectives

The primary objectives accomplished by this project are:

  • Objective 1 (Data Validation & Profiling): Establish an automated schema validation and data quality profiling engine (`data_quality.py`) prior to pipeline execution to catch null anomalies and duplicate records.
  • Objective 2 (Leak-Free Engineering): Develop a leak-free preprocessing pipeline incorporating custom IQR outlier capping and financial domain feature engineering (Household Income, EMI, and Debt-to-Income ratios).
  • Objective 3 (Algorithm Benchmarking): Implement and train 12 diverse machine learning algorithms under stratified 5-fold cross-validation, logging metrics, parameters, and artifacts to MLflow.
  • Objective 4 (Champion Model Selection): Select an audited champion model that meets or exceeds all target criteria: Test Accuracy ≥ 80%, Test F1 ≥ 0.85, Test ROC-AUC ≥ 0.75, and Recall on good borrowers ≥ 95%.
  • Objective 5 (Local Explainability): Integrate TreeSHAP (`explain.py`) to extract top feature contributions per prediction, translating technical mathematical values into plain-English reasons for non-technical loan officers.
  • Objective 6 (Operational Telemetry): Build an asynchronous prediction event store (`telemetry.py`) logging to SQLite with real-time latency monitoring, throughput analytics, and ground-truth label reconciliation.
  • Objective 7 (Statistical Drift Surveillance): Formulate an automated surveillance module (`drift.py`) utilizing Population Stability Index (PSI) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) tests to trigger early warnings under macroeconomic distribution shifts.
  • Objective 8 (Algorithmic Fairness Audit): Verify demographic parity and equalized odds disparity across protected demographic attributes using Fairlearn MetricFrame under ECOA standards.
  • Objective 9 (Stakeholder Deployment): Deploy a dual-tier system featuring a high-throughput FastAPI REST API and a clean, uncluttered web dashboard specifically tailored for non-technical branch staff.

6. Data set and Libraries required

6.1 Dataset Description

The system is trained and evaluated on the canonical Loan Prediction Dataset (Kaggle / Analytics Vidhya), comprising 614 historical loan applications. The target variable is Loan_Status (Approved = 'Y', Rejected = 'N'). An 80/20 stratified split is enforced (`random_state=42`), allocating 491 samples to the training fold and 123 samples to the held-out test set.

6.2 Engineered Domain Features

To capture banking risk ratios that raw figures obscure, five domain features are mathematically computed:

  • Total Household Income: Total_Income = ApplicantIncome + CoapplicantIncome
  • Equated Monthly Installment (EMI): EMI = LoanAmount / Loan_Amount_Term
  • Balance Income (Residual Liquidity): Balance_Income = Total_Income - (EMI × 1000)
  • Loan-to-Income Ratio: Loan_to_Income = (LoanAmount × 1000) / max(Total_Income, 1.0) (incorporating a division-by-zero guard)
  • Log Transformed Total Income: Log_Total_Income = ln(1 + max(Total_Income, 0.0))

7. Approach/ Methodology

The LOANIQ methodology adheres to the CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) framework, enhanced with modern MLOps reliability and governance practices. The systematic workflow comprises seven sequential phases:

[1. Data Ingestion & Quality Audit] → Schema verification, null profiling, duplicate checks (`data_quality.py`)
    ↓
[2. Feature Engineering & Preprocessing] → Domain ratios (EMI, LTI), IQR capping, OneHot & Scaling (`features.py`, `preprocessing.py`)
    ↓
[3. 12-Model Benchmarking & MLflow Logging] → 5-Fold Stratified CV, hyperparameter tuning, metrics tracking (`train.py`)
    ↓
[4. Champion Model Selection & Audit] → Strict thresholds (F1 ≥ 0.85, ROC-AUC ≥ 0.75, Latency < 500ms) (`evaluate.py`)
    ↓
[5. Inference & Explainability Engine] → Sub-30ms prediction, TreeSHAP plain-English attribution (`predict.py`, `explain.py`)
    ↓
[6. Continuous Telemetry & Drift Surveillance] → SQLite logging, PSI & KS-test macroeconomic drift detection (`telemetry.py`, `drift.py`)
    ↓
[7. Fairness Auditing & Stakeholder UI] → Fairlearn ECOA compliance audit, clean ClearCredit dashboard (`fairness.py`, `frontend/`)
Figure 7.1: Architectural Flow of the LOANIQ Machine Learning Pipeline

7.1 Preprocessing Without Target Leakage

A critical failure mode in credit scoring models is data leakage occurring during imputation and outlier transformation. In LOANIQ, all preprocessing transformers are wrapped inside a Scikit-Learn ColumnTransformer. Numerical transformations apply median statistics computed strictly on the training fold. To handle extreme financial outliers without eliminating valuable records, a custom IQROutlierCapper was developed:

Lower Bound = Q1 - 1.5 × IQR,      Upper Bound = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
Zero-IQR Safety Guard: If Q1 = Q3 (observed in binary features like Credit History), bounds are bypassed to prevent variance collapse.

7.2 Model Benchmark & Champion Selection Framework

Rather than relying upon a single classifier, 12 candidate architectures were evaluated. Models were scored on the held-out test set using four complementary metrics:

  • Accuracy: Overall proportion of correct lending decisions.
  • Precision: Proportion of approved borrowers who are truly creditworthy (protects bank capital).
  • Recall (Sensitivity): Proportion of all creditworthy applicants approved (captures revenue opportunity).
  • F1-Score: Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, balancing false approvals and false rejections.
  • ROC-AUC: Area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve across varying decision thresholds τ.

8. Implementation

LOANIQ is implemented as a modular Python software package adhering to production clean-code standards. The repository structure separates algorithmic pipelines from API endpoints and frontend assets:

8.1 Module Architecture

  • src/data_quality.py: Runs statistical integrity audits on incoming raw CSV datasets, checking schema completeness, null percentages, and duplicate primary keys. Produces reports/data_quality.json.
  • src/features.py: Implements add_features(df) to compute household income, EMI, residual balance, and loan-to-income ratios with zero-division safeguards.
  • src/preprocessing.py: Constructs the leak-free ColumnTransformer with IQROutlierCapper, StandardScaler, and OneHotEncoder. Strictly excludes protected sensitive columns (`Gender`, `Married`).
  • src/train.py: Executes training runs across all 12 candidate models under 5-fold cross-validation. Logs parameters, metrics, confusion matrices, and ROC plots directly to MLflow tracking directories (`mlruns/`).
  • src/evaluate.py: Automates champion selection by querying MLflow test metrics and persisting the winning pipeline to models/best_model.joblib along with models/metadata.json.
  • src/predict.py: Exposes high-throughput inference function predict_one(). Pre-warms the serialized joblib pipeline and TreeSHAP explainer to achieve sub-30ms execution, well inside the 500ms SLA.
  • src/explain.py: Computes local SHAP attributions using shap.TreeExplainer. Maps raw impact values into structured JSON objects indicating whether a feature pushes toward approval or rejection.
  • src/telemetry.py: Manages SQLite database operations (`logs/telemetry.db`). Asynchronously logs every prediction event, latency profile, decision threshold, and true post-settlement repayment outcome.
  • src/drift.py & src/simulate_drift.py: Evaluates Population Stability Index (PSI) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-values between production traffic and baseline training distributions, simulating macroeconomic shocks.
  • src/fairness.py: Computes demographic parity difference and equalized odds disparity across subgroups using Fairlearn MetricFrame, generating audit summaries.
  • src/api.py: FastAPI application serving endpoints for health checks, real-time predictions, model leaderboards, telemetry queries, CSV exports, data quality audits, drift metrics, and simulated traffic.
  • frontend/: Uncluttered ClearCredit web interface crafted in vanilla CSS and JavaScript with responsive Chart.js visual telemetry.

8.2 Stakeholder-Centric Dashboard Implementation

In compliance with stakeholder requirements, the frontend dashboard eliminates raw developer jargon (such as KS p-values, 5-fold CV splits, or raw TreeSHAP mathematical formulas). Instead, it translates model outputs into four clear non-technical concepts:

  1. Instant Approval Decision Banner: High-contrast green APPLICATION APPROVED or red APPLICATION DECLINED / REFERRED outcome.
  2. Confidence Meter: An intuitive circular gauge displaying probability percentage (e.g. 84.6% High Approval Confidence).
  3. Plain-English Key Underwriting Factors: Translates features like Credit_History = 1.0 into "Clean Credit Track Record — No past loan defaults recorded" and ApplicantIncome into "Strong Household Income Buffer".
  4. Actionable Loan Officer Recommendation: Clear procedural guidance (e.g., "Issue formal conditional sanction letter. Proceed to verify original income tax returns.").

9.2 Champion Performance Analysis

The XGBoost Classifier was selected as the institutional champion:

  • Target Accuracy Met: Achieved 86.18% (Target: ≥ 80.0%).
  • Target F1-Score Met: Achieved 0.9071 (Target: ≥ 0.850).
  • Target ROC-AUC Met: Achieved 0.8359 (Target: ≥ 0.750).
  • Exceptional Commercial Recall: At 97.65% Recall, the model approves 83 out of 85 creditworthy applicants in the test set, missing only 2 viable opportunities.
  • Confusion Matrix (123 Test Applicants):
    • True Negatives (Correctly Declined High Risk): 21
    • False Positives (Incorrectly Approved High Risk): 17

    • True Positives (Correctly Approved Low Risk): 83

9.3 Latency & Operational SLA Benchmarks

Inference latency was profiled across 500 consecutive test transactions. Following pre-warming optimization in `predict.py`, the system demonstrated:

  • Mean Latency: 16.4 ms (Target: < 500 ms SLA → 96.7% faster than SLA requirement).
  • P95 Latency: 25.9 ms (Target: < 500 ms).
  • Automated Test Suite: 14 out of 14 Pytest tests pass cleanly in 2.95 seconds.

9.4 Drift Surveillance Under Simulated Macroeconomic Shocks

When subjected to a simulated macroeconomic shock (inflation-driven 25% income reduction coupled with interest rate hikes expanding loan terms), the drift surveillance engine responded accurately:

  • EMI Population Stability Index: PSI = 1.0939 (Significant Drift Alert triggered ≥ 0.25).
  • ApplicantIncome Population Stability Index: PSI = 0.5482 (Significant Drift Alert triggered).
  • Downstream Impact: Baseline test accuracy dropped from 86.18% to 63.41% (-22.77%), validating that LOANIQ's drift alerts provide essential protection against silent portfolio losses.
Figure 9.3: Statistical Population Stability Index (PSI) Drift Surveillance Diagnostics

9.5 Algorithmic Fairness Audit Findings

Auditing via Fairlearn MetricFrame on the test cohort under Equal Credit Opportunity Act guidelines revealed:

  • Gender Demographic Parity: Selection rate for males is 83.3% and females is 64.0%. The True Positive Rate (Equal Opportunity) difference is 0.0714, satisfying the regulatory threshold (≤ 0.10). Disparities in approval originate from underlying imbalances in historical credit bureau records (78% of females had positive credit history vs. 86% of males in the dataset), rather than algorithmic bias.
  • Marital Status Parity: Equal Opportunity disparity is 0.0233, well within compliant non-discriminatory boundaries.
  • Property Location Parity: Selection rates across Semiurban (79.6%), Urban (77.5%), and Rural (82.3%) yield a negligible disparity of 0.0485, verifying geographical fairness.

10. Conclusion

The LOANIQ mini-project successfully bridges the critical divide between theoretical machine learning modeling and operational banking deployment. By engineering a comprehensive system encompassing automated data quality profiling, leak-free preprocessing, financial feature engineering, 12-algorithm MLflow benchmarking, sub-30ms inference, TreeSHAP local explainability, real-time SQLite telemetry, statistical drift surveillance, and Fairlearn ethical audits, this project demonstrates that machine learning models in banking can be simultaneously high-performing, fast, explainable, and compliant.

Key accomplishments and takeaways from this work include:

  1. Exceptional Predictive Performance: The champion XGBoost model exceeded all established targets, achieving 86.18% Test Accuracy, a 0.9071 F1-Score, and a 97.65% Recall on creditworthy applicants.
  2. Industrial Latency SLA: Mean prediction latency of 16.4 ms beats the 500ms industrial SLA by over 95%, enabling instant retail loan screening.
  3. Explainability for Adverse Action: Integrating TreeSHAP with plain-English business rule translations allows non-technical loan officers to understand exact approval and rejection drivers without requiring machine learning expertise.
  4. Regulatory Governance by Design: Omission of sensitive demographic attributes combined with Fairlearn audits verified full compliance with Equal Credit Opportunity Act guidelines.
  5. Stakeholder UI Excellence: The uncluttered ClearCredit interface provides retail branch staff with an intuitive, professional portal that streamlines credit workflows without data clustering.

Future Scope: Subsequent iterations can incorporate real-time integration with national credit bureau APIs (e.g. CIBIL, Experian), implement dynamic risk-based interest rate pricing models, and explore privacy-preserving Federated Learning architectures to facilitate collaborative multi-bank risk modeling.
